speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs):	Mr. Speaker, I must crave your indulgence for referring again today to thie matter of Polish treasures. I do not wish to prolong the controversy, but it is only proper that all the facts be placed before the public so that they may have their own views as to their proper interpretation1.
Press statements have been called to my attention in which it is said that the Polish charge d'affaires in Canadia wrote to the Mother Superior of the Hotel Dieu in Quebec city stating, amongst other things that the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had been placed at his disposal to recover the art treasures which were said to be stored at that place. I have no direct knowledge of this communication or of any other communications which the Polish charge d'affaires may have addressed to private individuals in Canada. It is not true, however, that any undertaking was given to the representative of the Polish government in Canada, either orally or in writing, by myself or any official of the Canadian government, to the effect that the services of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would be placed at his disposal. He was informed only that, in order that he and his solicitors might undertake any legal proceedings they thought appropriate, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would be asked to endeavour to ascertain the location of the missing articles. In order that there may be no misapprehension on this subject, I am quoting the relevant part of the letter in which the charge d'affaires of the Polish legation was informed of the location of the articles which had been stored in Quebec City.
The portion of the letter, signed by the under-secretary of state is as follows- -

subtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT-FURTHER STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
What date?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have not the date, but it was just as soon as we got the information that these articles had been located in the city of Quebec. It states:
I have now been informed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that certain Polish art treasures which were brought to Canada by ithe Polish authorities in 1940 and which subsequently disappeared have mow been located at l'Hotel Dieu, Quebec city, Quebec. The articles at this location are said to be contained in twenty-three trunks and one wooden box and to have been stored previously at the Redemp-torist Monastery at Ste. Anne de Beaupre.
As we agreed with your solicitors, we are communicating the information to you for any further action you and your solicitors may wish to take.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked for the production of certain papers. He said:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the minister admits that the mounted police were used for civil purposes, he can have no objection to producing the reports given by Corporal Car-riere and Constable Houle, either bo himself as Minister of External Affairs or to the Minister of Justice, and I would ask whether or not those reports will be tabled.
Later he said:
Them I would ask the Minister of Justice whether he would produce these reports, because they deal with a civil matter, and the mounted police do not deal with civil matters.
To which I replied:
I shall be glad to give consideration to my hon. friend's request and give him an answer tomorrow. I am strongly under the impression that police reports to the commissioner, if there are any, are not under any circumstances producible in this house.
I find that there were certain reports from these two members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to their superiors but that they were of a confidential character and were so marked, and I therefore must decline to produce those reports on the ground of public interest.
I have not been able to find any indication in the authorities that anything turns on the distinction my hon. friend made yesterday between police activities in criminal matters and in civil matters. If anything did turn
Polish Art Treasures

on that, the same rule would clearly apply to reports made in civil matters. I quote from Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, page 251:
The practice of asking for reports from officers, addressed to particular departments of the executive government, is considered to be open to serious objection. As to "confidential documents" passing between officers of a department, Mr. Speaker Peel observes: "They are not necessarily laid on the table of the house, especially if the minister declares that they aye of a confidential character." He adds: "that if a minister stated in his place that a document was of that class, the house should tajie his word, and he was not bound to lay it on the table.
The observations which apply in that citation to reports from officers of a department apply a fortiori to reports from members of the police forces to their superiors, and it would be clearly contrary to the public interest to produce such secret and confidential reports or lay them on the table of the House of Commons.

subtopic: POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT-FURTHER STATEMENT OF SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, when the minister states that it is not in the public interest to produce the papers I believe his statement must be accepted; but when he says that there is no authority for it and that it has not been asked before in parliament I must say that the Prime Minister himself, when leader of the opposition on July 2, 1935, at page 4133 of Hansard asked for the production in this house of certain instructions given to the mounted police of that day, and himself desired the production of those papers. As a matter of fact-and I want to be frank- the answer given by the Prime Minister then was that he did not think they were producible. It is fair enough to say that; and I cannot find that it was discussed later. But certainly in 1935 the present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition thought it only proper to produce them.
While we are speaking about production, sir, I would suggest, being bound by what the Minister of Justice says, that possibly the Secretary of State for External Affairs, having chosen selected portions of a letter a few moments ago, will now table in the house the entire letter or state paper, as the case may be, because of citation 315, which I shall now read:
A minister of the crown is no.t at liberty to read or quote from a dispatch or other state paper not before the house, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the table.
He has referred to one of the documents that I had in mind, and I suggest, sir, that he now be asked to table the entire letter from which he read a selected extract.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I have not the letter here; I shall give the request made by the hon. member for Lake Centre very sympathetic consideration.

subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) referred to a telegram he had received from the secretary of the Retail Merchants Association of Alberta relating to the matter of commercial rentals, and suggesting that authority be retained by the rentals division of the board to deal with each case on its merits when application for a board ruling is made by a tenant. He asked me if I would give the matter consideration and make a statement with regard to the request.
I would say now with respect to the commercial rentals situation that there still remains in order in council PC. 9029, the wartime leasehold regulations, section 6, subsection 1, which makes it an offence for any person to charge a rental which is higher than is reasonable and just.
As the government is continuing rental control on housing accommodation, it is necessary that this section remain in effect.
This section has general application; accordingly, it remains an offence for a landlord to charge a rental for commercial space that is clearly unreasonable and unjust. Should any such case be brought to the attention of the wartime prices and trade board, investigation will be made.
Hon. members will realize that it is unusually difficult to assess the value of commercial accommodation because so much depends upon the value of the site, nature of the business carried on, and the volume of business attributable to the location.
It must be also remembered that rent control of commercial space has now been in effect for over six and a half years. During this time many locations which in 1941 had little commercial value have now become quite valuable for one reason or another. Because of these factors previous maximum rentals in effect are not necessarily relevant in determining the reasonableness of the rentals now being asked.
Since December 1, 1945, the law has permitted a landlord to enter into a lease with an existing tenant at a rental that was mutually satisfactory to both parties, provided that the term of the lease was for a period of five years or longer and the lease contained

Rent Control
no predetermination clause. The five-year period was reduced to a three-year period in the spring of 1947. It would not be the government's intention to examine into the rentals reserved under these leases, as these were lawful rentals.

subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: I take it it is clear that it will continue to be the responsibility of the wartime prices and trade board to enforce the provisions of section 6 (1) of the wartime leasehold regulations with respect to unreasonable and unjust projects.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: I believe I can answer that in this way, that if it is clearly established that a rental which is unreasonable and unjust is being charged the board would consider taking a prosecution. It is open under the section for anyone to do it, with the consent of the board or with the consent of a provincial attorney general. I am not prepared to say now to what extent the board should be or would be prepared to undertake the task of prosecutions. What I have said, in effect, is that if cases of that kind are brought to the attention of the board, investigations will be made.

subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? Does the board have power to reduce rentals, or can it merely prosecute?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: It can only prosecute.

subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? The minister said that if it was clearly established that the rent was unreasonable and unjust, certain action would be taken. How is that to be established before it can be brought to the attention of the wartime prices and trade board?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps I should put'it this way. Presumably the tenant would be in the best position to decide whether he thinks the rent is unreasonable and unjust. He could complain, I assume, to the wartime prices and trade board. An investigation would be made and the investigator would come to a conclusion one way or the other. If he came to the conclusion that it was clearly unreasonable and unjust I assume that the board would institute proper proceedings. I have stated that the board will investigate complaints of this kind to the extent of its capacity.

subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: As I understand it, this will have nothing to do with the right of the landlord to evict his tenant. The only remedy suggested now is that the tenant may prosecute if the rental fixed is considered unreasonable and unjust-or is it "or unjust"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: And.

subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have had this phrase in our legislation for a long time. I am sure no one appreciates more than the minister the difficulty of basing a prosecution upon words of general application such as "unreasonable and unjust". I was wondering if the board had had any success in prosecutions of the kind, realizing as I do the great difficulty of asking a tribunal to decide. Perhaps some refinement might be made in that term, or more definite words used, so that in the event of the proper authorities launching a prosecution they would have some hope of succeeding. This is like asking what is the size of the chancellor's boot, or something of the kind. It is a very broad phrase, and I am inclined to think that it would be difficult to enforce a regulation under those words as they stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DECONTROL OF COMMERCIAL RENTS-WARTIME LEASEHOLD REGULATIONS
speechtext: Answering the first question, I understand that before the over-all ceilings were applied early in the war there were two, or possibly three, prosecutions under the "unjust and unreasonable" clause, and I understand there were two convictions. Then the over-all ceilings were put on and a breach of the price ceiling automatically was considered to be selling at a price which was unjust and unreasonable.

maintopic: PROPOSED REMOVAL OP COMMERCIAL RENT CONTROLS -MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, seconded by the hon. member for Melfort, has moved for leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 31 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance. Hon. members know that it is the practice to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance when under the orders of the day they would have no opportunity to discuss it. In a few minutes from now, according to the business of the house which was decided last night, the house will proceed to debate the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Hon. members know perfectly well that in the course of that debate it will be their privilege to discuss any matter. Therefore I do not see why I should permit the adjournment of the house to discuss this matter when the house will have an opportunity to discuss it in a few minutes.

maintopic: PROPOSED REMOVAL OP COMMERCIAL RENT CONTROLS -MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: On a point of order, I cannot find anything in standing order 31 which provides for this sort of adjournment, which says that if there is an occasion on which the matter can be discussed the motion should not be granted. If the debate on the address goes on, there is no assurance that the hon. member who wants to raise this question will be able to speak. This question either stands or falls on its own merits as a question of urgent public importance, and in my. opinion it cannot be sidetracked by saying that there is an opportunity to discuss it in some other debate. It is a question which stands by itself and which must be decided according to the rules as they appear in Beauchesne's rules and orders.

maintopic: PROPOSED REMOVAL OP COMMERCIAL RENT CONTROLS -MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext: The hon. member will understand that I cannot enter into a debate on the ruling which I have given. It is a well known fact that a member may ask leave to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance. The idea of permitting such a motion is to enable hon. members to discuss urgent matters of public importance when they have no other opportunity to do so. But in a few minutes from now, as I have already said, the debate on the address will be before the house, and it will be the privilege of members to discuss any matter in that debate. I am sorry, therefore, mat I cannot accept the hon. member's motion.

The particular reason for my taking part in this debate is a short speech which was made last night by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). I am not disputing in any way his right to make that speech, but his doing so affected what has become the general procedure in these formal debates. As a rule the whips know how many speakers there are to be from each group; the Speaker gets a list and from that list he recognizes the various speakers in turn. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) took the floor he did some fancy skating which I do not believe could be excelled, if equalled, by the young lady from Ottawa who is at present overseas and has done such a splendid job in her field for Canada. The leader of the opposition drew a very fine distinction. In view of some of the things that happen occasionally, Mr. Speaker, the ability of the leader of the opposition to draw fine distinctions will some day eminently fit him to be Speaker of this house, although I hope the time never comes when
his group will be elected with a sufficient majority to place him in that position. But he has that qualification, if none other.

marketing as the organized farmers want it. We believe in prices for agricultural products that will bring the farming community its share of the national income according to its numerical strength. We believe, and we so stated in 1945 and at every other opportunity we had, and I state it again now, that while we believe in that, we believe also in the other types of controls which make those stabilized prices worthwhile tc the farmer in bringing to him that share of the national income to which we believe he is entitled. They believe in their position in society, and they are defending that position. They believe that their position in society is so great that they are entitled to have a pool of unemployment. I have read in a businessman's magazine a statement that burnt its way right into my soul. I have lived very little of my life outside, except when I have travelled to see something else. I have no intention of leaving Canada, because I like it. But I do not want Canada to be compared with other countries. I only want to make this comparison: What is Canada capable of doing and what is she doing? If these things compare favourably I am agreeable; if they compare unfavourably I am not agreeable and will continue trying to have them favourable. I state that even though we have made advances under our democracy, and have made many improvements-I would be the last one to deny it-there are still many things more we want to have done; and if I thought it was of any use, Mr. Speaker, I would change my tone from accusation to one of pleading. I would beg of these people who so far have represented one or the other type of government that we have had here, and both of which mean the same thing, to change their course, stop taking their orders from the Canadian chamber of commerce and start
The Address-Mr. Bentley

taking suggestions from the farm organizations and the labour organizations in this country.
If I thought it would produce any softening of their hearts, any lessening of their desire to be the bosses of mankind, to be the brass hats and established bureaucrats by divine right; if I thought anything would make them feel that way I would plead with them, even though it robbed me of dignity. I would gladly relinquish dignity in the interests of my fellow-Canadian wage earners and farmers.
That is very touching.
We take suggestions from our constituents.
And from the Canadian chamber of commerce.

There have been a few minor things and one major thing done that organized farmers asked for. Organized farmers asked for years for wheat and grains to be marketed by the Canadian wheat board, but the government refused from 1935 until September, 1943, to do this, and then only did it because a situation, in the transportation field during those war years made it imperative. It was not done at the request of the organized farmers. I know that story too well. The government has done some minor things, but in the major fields it has yet to do anything, and I will now mention some of them. I wish I could deal with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Redi Deer (Mr. Shaw). There was a great deal of it that I would have been happy to support, but unfortunately I shall not be able to deal with that as I should have liked to. We would have been glad to have supported it, even though it did not do all the things

that we would like done, nor did it do those-things that would have been done under it in ways that we would have liked best. But,, unlike the leader of the opposition, we are too-anxious to see come out of this debate some good for the Canadian- people to quibble about little things, and we are not prepared to allow some political differences to prevent us from assisting another political party with a good: idea along the lines we believe in.

So far it has not been granted to me and, according to the doctor's advice, unless an accident happens I am not likely to achieve that in the near future. Will the hon. member permit a question? I was going to ask the hon. member whether he was aware that there were two coalitions in British Columbia. The Address-Mr. Bentley
That is a lie.
It is not a lie.
There is no such thing.
The L.P.P. collected money for the C.C.F., and the only thing that made the C.C.F. mad was that they could not get their hands on it.
A coalition requires agreement. There is repudiation on our part.

He is just not mature.

In the amendment moved by the hon. member for Red Deer there are a number of things that we would have liked to see. We believe that the things contained in the first paragraph are absolutely essential to this country, and if it is out of order to move them as an amendment or a subamendment to the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne, then I hope the government will at least take note of them and start to set up machinery to put them into operation. We could agree with paragraph (b), although I would have wished that he had added a little bit more to it; because in paragraph (b) he suggested the elimination of the sales tax and substantial reductions in excise, processing and all other hidden and nuisance taxes. I wish he had added in there, a substantial reduction in the existing excise tax and an undertaking that no new excise taxes will be imposed by the proposed legislation which we were told last night will follow this debate.
To impose an excise profit tax.

Yes. Turning to paragraphs (c) and (d), we would have liked to see that a little more extensive to include a number of other people. For instance, we would have liked to see it include veterans -on pension, veterans dependents, and veterans on war veterans allowance. In that connection I would have liked! to see veterans on veterans allowance paid* their allowance,
' regardless of whether they live in Canada or in foreign lands. Some of our veterans whose pensions are small, but who have reached the age of sixty entitling them to war veterans allowance, because of the condition of their health have to live in Arizona or some place else, are unable to get war veterans allowance.
I think that is a restriction that is absolutely unfair. I would have liked to see the provision I mentioned included there. \Ve would have liked to see the non-pensioned war widows included and pensions for the spouses of all old age pensioners, even though the spouse is younger than the pension age required.
We regret that the speech from the throne did not contain any suggestion that there were to be amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, to make it more equitable, that it be paid on an individual basis. There was no suggestion in the speech from the throne that the government intends to set up a federal co-operative act. Everybody loves it. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) says he fathers it and has all through the years; but when it comes to the point of doing something about it, actually to breathe some life into whatever he has produced so far, nothing has taken place. We should like to see that. We should like to see a federal marketing act. I could spend quite a bit of time in telling why we want it, but the agricultural people of western Canada want it. badly.

Mr. GEORGES-H. HEON (Argenteuil): Mr. Speaker, although the fact may annoy and irritate those of a fanatical and narrow turn of mind, and recent happenings show that, unfortunately, such people are still found among us. Canada officially recognizes two languages, French and English, granting to both equal rights and equal consideration and making neither dependent to the other.
Therefore, if I choose to express myself in the language spoken by the discoverers of this country, I need neither apologize nor ask
The Address-Mr. Neon

anyone's permission. Some lion, members within hearing may perhaps not have the opportunity or the good fortune of speaking or understanding the French language, but if they are steeped in the history of our country and in the principles of etiquette and courtesy, they will respect the sacred rights of the language I am proud to use and allow me to speak without interrupting me. This is a purely hypothetical suggestion, but should the audience number some ignorant, and intoxicated noisemakers hating everything that is French, they would doubtless attempt to silence me, thus giving vent to their contemptible feelings, by using the trick of gibbering and incomprehensible interruption, or by raising some useful but well-worn technical objection.
In the latter case, all those who, like me, cannot disown the blood which flows in their veins and recall with pride their French origin, would leap in anger at this insult and remind interrupters in plain language that as long as there remains one French-speaking Canar dian in this country and one French-speaking member in this house, the French tongue will be spoken, honoured and respected.
We are neither poor relations nor valets nor a conquered people in this country of ours, in any of the provinces or in this house, but equal partners and associates.
There is ample evidence in the political history of Canada to show that Canadians of French origin have always acted in a spirit of conciliation, very often to their own detriment. They have always expressed a sincere wish to work in harmony with their fellow-countrymen of other races in building a strong, united and autonomous Canadian nation. But they are firmly resolved that their right to speak their own language anywhere should be respected. There can be no compromise on this point.
Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate, fortunately drawing to a close, we have heard many speeches. Some have been excellent, such as the one delivered by my hon. friend; from Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr, Dion); others were open to criticism. I wish to refer briefly to the speech of the hon. member for Gaspe given on Monday March 1, 1948, and which Le Devoir of March 2, 1948, described as a "bad speech" acompanying a "bad deed." In his all-out attack which undoubtedly caused the absentees concerned to tremble with fear, the speaker directed his big electoral guns against Messrs. Duplessis, Sauve and Chaloult. He was particularly critical of

certain parts of the two latters' speeches. It is rather surprising that the official opposition in the Legislative Assembly did not elaborate further on the member for Gaspe's speech and follow suit. They have there,, indeed some dangerous challengers and we shall await impatiently to hear from the hon. Mr. Godbout and Jos. Francoeur. They will oppose Mr. Chaloult cn immigration and civil service and Mr. Sauve on the subject of Canada's war effort.
As for the criticism directed by the hon. member at the Hon. Paul Sauve's remarks, let me remind him of a thing or two, even though I have no intention of embarrassing him with certain unpleasant memories. Not far away from where he sits in this chamber there are some supporters of the government, who, during the sessions of 1939, 1940, 1941, 1942, 1943 and especially 1944, when conscription had to be voted by the government of the day, were most bitter in their condemnation of our participation and used much more violent language in speaking of their own leaders than did Mr. Sauve. If my hon. friend and those who sit with him, wish to criticize the speeches which may have been made on the part we played in the war, why does he not begin by cleaning up the ranks of his own friends, if he is so exasperated by criticism of our war effort? He could find all the subject-matter he could wish to speak on if he were only to consult the official report for those sessions. If he cannot find it, I shall only be too happy to give him the reference in a subsequent speech.
(Text):
As I rise to address the house briefly, Mr. Speaker, may I immediately, both on my own behalf and on behalf of the population of the historic constituency of Argenteuil which I am proud to represent in this parliament, pay a most respectful tribute to the memory of a distinguished Canadian, the late Lady Perley, wife of my immediate predecessor the Right Hon. Sir George Halsey Perley.
Lady Perley spent her life in promoting, encouraging and supporting, financially and otherwise, innumerable social, charitable and welfare organizations, particularly in her own city of Ottawa w'hich she loved and served so faithfully and well.
During the long period while her husband acted as federal member for Argenteuil, Lady Perley took a very active interest in the social, educational and economic welfare of the constituents of Argenteuil. And while Sir George Perley acted as high commissioner in

The Address-Mr. Heon
London, and overseas minister of militia during the first great war, Lady Perley gave unstintingly of her time and money to entertain the Canadian troops at Canada House in London and, generally, to assure their welfare through the various auxiliary services, as many old veterans will surely recall.
It is not unfair to affirm that the distinction, the charm and the devotion of Lady Perley contributed immensely to the splendid achievements of her distinguished husband in the realm of public and social services to his fellow-countrymen. The Perley name will ever remain beloved and respected in the constituency' of Argenteuil and in the city of Ottawa, although both "Sir George", as he was affectionately called, and his devoted wife, have passed away.
The speech from the throne contains a thinly-veiled warning as to the dangers of the international situation, and it is evident that all classes of our population have become keenly worried and anxious as to the possibilities of another conflict. I trust that very soon the government will make a clear and positive statement of the true situation that exists so that the country will know definitely, as is its absolute right, whether there will be an enduring peace, a cold war or another armed conflict: There is no need or place for an iron curtain in Canada.
Be that as it may, one must strain his imagination considerably to remain optimistic as to the ultimate alternative which can only be a choice between serfdom and freedom. When I speak of freedom I speak of the only true freedom which was implanted in the soul of man by his Creator, a freedom built on the spiritual destiny of mankind, freedom for which a son of God died on Calvary. Let us not prostitute the word "freedom". It has never meant licence and lawlessness, seditious utterance or conspiracy against religion, consti-uted authority, our Christian way of life, our free institutions. We pray it will never mean the exploitation of the many by the few, of the poor by the rich, of the humble by the mighty, of labour by capital or of capital by labour.
Thus, whilst in our midst we are whittling away our freedom and squabbling as to its true meaning, the forces of evil and serfdom- they are one and the same-are rolling westward in Europe and eastward in Asia. Here is the score as, in baseball parlance, we go to bat after the disastrous Czechoslovakian inning. I shall refer first to Poland. However, because Poland has come to the fore on account of the hidden treasure episode, I do not intend to rely upon my own opinion, but rather will I quote from outstanding authorities, the first being Raymond Leslie Buell, adviser to Time Incorporated on foreign affairs. He wrote the following which appeared in the American Mercury of March, 1946:
If world war II has any meaning it is that the people of Poland and other victims of axis aggression should have the right to choose their way of life and their economic and political system. But this right has been denied to the people of Poland. Today they are being subjected to a reign of terror imposed by a communist minority backed by Russian force. Those Poles who believe in the independence of their country are systematically being liquidated. It is my considered judgment that the present fate of Poland is one of the great outrages of history.
Gladwin Hill of the New York Times, after a visit to Poland, wrote the following which appeared in the New York Times of October 17 and 24, 1947:
Behind the facade of a "coalition?' government consisting of four "fake" parties, Poland today is ruled by three communists, members of the old Comintern and. citizens of foreign countries. These are Bodeslaw Bierut, president of the national council, a citizen of Soviet Russia, Wladyslaw Gomolka, vice premier of Poland but a citizen of France, and Stanislaw Rad-kiewicz, minister of public security, a man who hardly knows Polish and who is a high official in the soviet political police. In fact, soviet employees, who are unseen from the outside, are in charge of all Polish governmental agencies.
There exists in Poland a "subtle reign of terror" with possibly 100,000 political prisoners in jails and concentration camps, whose only offence is opposition to the "current communist dominated regime." Poland is in the throes of an intense political struggle. It is a struggle led by Moscow trained communists to get permanent political control of a country that is historically conservative. The Russian troops which stand back of this communist dominated regime are stripping Poland of industrial plants, cattle and numerous other articles, thereby deepening terrible economic distress.
Finally, this is a quotation from R. H. Mackham, Balkan expert of the Christian Science Monitor, who writes:
Bodeslaw Bierut, one of the leaders of the third international, is the despot of Poland.
Is it small wonder then, in view of these statements, that some of us, much like the nuns of the Hotel Dieu, are wary of striking a bargain with these individuals?
Let us consult again our score cards:
In Yugoslavia, Joseph Broz, another member of the third international, is the absolute dictator.
In Hungary, Maty Rakosi, still another member of the third international, has stolen from and robbed, Hungarians of their freedom.
In Roumania, Alma Pauker, woman member of the third international, is the undisputed boss of 16,000,000 Roumanians.
The Address-Mr. Heon

In Bulgaria, George Dimi-troff, leading member of the third international, is the master of 8,000,000 Bulgarians.
In Austria, Ernst Fisher
In eastern Germany, Wilham Piech
In Italy, Togliatti
In France, Thorez
In Finland, Kuusinen
In Greece, Zaehairiades and Villafides
In China, Mao-tse-tsung
are all members of the third communist international and are plotting day and night to turn over their country to the forces of evil and the enemies of freedom.
Does the hon. member say that Togliatti and Thorez are the chief communistic authorities in Italy and France?

I have not made that statement. I have said and repeated that Thorez in France and Togliatti in Italy, with others, are working towards the establishment of communist-dominated regimes in those two countries.
That is what I wanted to know.
Are we agreed?
Yes.

Thank you.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there is Czechoslovakia. What a tragedy, yet what a lesson for all countries still remaining free! Mr. Benes and his associates failed to listen to the advice of those who warned him that one cannot serve God and Satan, and he chose instead to negotiate, to compromise, and to trust those evil forces whose amoral code is based on treachery, deceit, liquidation and the obliteration of Christianity, decency and freedom. Where do Mr. Benes and the Czechoslovakian population find themselves today? Exactly where all other nations and individuals have found themselves when they trusted and believed in the lies and cajoleries of the Marxian and Leninist enemies of Christian- freedom.
But, tragic and regrettable as the Czechoslovakian robbery may be, it will serve some purpose if it is taken as a final warning by those governments and peoples in all the lands where the light of freedom still remains unextinguished. Shall our own country, Canada, ever become infested with or subservient to these same atheistic, destructive forces? The answer will be in the negative, provided that -we rededicate ourselves to the cause of Christian freedom and see to it that we do not foster religious, racial or cldss hatred. Marxism and Leninism can never take root in a country where the people go reverently 
and regularly to church, draw adequate wTages, are properly housed and educated, and are free to move and do as they please; but insufficient wages, profiteering, slums and ignorance are the breeding grounds of bloody revolutions and the dictatorship of the proletariat.	.
It is then the duty of everyone of us here, Mr. Speaker, to proclaim freedom; but that is not sufficient. We must always legislate and administer to sustain and extend freedom.

was paired. Had I voted, I would have voted against the amendment.

It has been intimated to me during the past several hours that a number of government members are profoundly sorry that they have been deprived of the opportunity of supporting my subamendment.
Name them.

During the last several weeks speeches which have emanated from that quarter have indicated that hon. members are conscious of the fact that the electors back home are, in the first place, dissatisfied with the prevailing high rate of taxation. They are dissatisfied with the low exemptions at
present in force under the Income War Tax Act. Hon. gentlemen have also indicated that their electors are demanding the elimination of the sales tax. They have indicated their realization that demands back home are also being made for reductions in the excise tax and in other taxes as well. A number of them have referred to the necessity of making revisions in the Family Allowance Act, in some instances for the purpose of removing anomalies and in other cases for the purpose of making larger payments under that act.
Certain hon. members have seen fit to rise in their places and protest against the shabby treatment which is still being accorded our pioneer citizens. I have heard many of them protest against the eligibility age as being far too high. I have heard many of them protest against the means test. They have also lifted their voices in opposition to the fact that the wife of a pensioner, if she is under seventy years of age, is not at present eligible for a pension.
Many statements have come from quarters opposite, sympathetic toward disabled persons in this country who, in consequence of their disabilities, are unable to secure a decent standard of living. Moreover, we have heard assertions in support of certain subsidies, selected subsidies, if I may call them that, which would have the effect of reducing living costs for many of our people.
It is a fact that the people of Canada, and more especially those in the lower income tax brackets, have been pleading with the government for relief from the very great burden of living costs under which they at present suffer. This heavy burden has resulted directly from government policy or, I might say, from the actions of men. It can be eased-there is no question about it-and made more bearable by immediate changes in policy. Hon. gentlemen on the front benches opposite are the only ones who are in a position to make those changes.
The people of Canada, in overwhelming majority, have demanded lower living costs. We know, as members of parliament, the number of communications we have received in this respect. Many of our people have been, led to believe that the only method by which we can reduce these living costs is through the reimposition of price controls. The government has taken the position that in peacetime the people of Canada would not submit to an overall system of price controls, and we have admitted that perhaps the government is right in that stand. But this does not mean that there is not another way of effecting the same result, namely, a lowering of living costs for Canadians.
The Address-Mr. Shaw

I should like to point out that since the government considers it impractical to reimpose price controls, then- the logical thing is for it to approach the matter from another point of view. If the government cannot bring down prices so as to make it possible for all Canadians to enjoy a decent standard of living, it can surely go a long way toward establishing at least a minimum income for all Canadians, an income that will furnish that decent standard of living. The government stands condemned in- the eyes of the Canadian people. Why? For its failure to take the action which could achieve that result, namely, the lowering of living costs and the establishment of a decent standard of living.
Some specific things the government could have done are embodied in the amendment to the motion which I should like to move. Before moving it, I should like to say this. The amendment is not intended to be by any means a complete list, but at least it does indicate a method by which the government of Canada could reduce the living costs of all Canadians by at least twenty per cent. At the same time I am sure that the government could be dispensing something like social justice for thousands of our aged people, for our veterans and their dependents, and for the blind and helpless adults who are now without an adequate means of support. So, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), that the following be added to the motion:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers should have given- assurance to this house that legislation would be submitted during the present session, whereby the following results wo-uld be achieved, as a contribution towards- meeting -the crisis in living costs, and towards stabilizing the Canadian economy:
(a)	Exemption from income tax on incomes of married persons of $2,400 and less, and of single persons of $1,500; these to be progressively increased to $3,000 and $2,0-00 as production increases in relation to demand.
(b)	Elimination of the sales tax, and substantial reduction in excise, processing -and all other hidden and n-uisance taxes.
(c)	Substantial^ increases in family allowances; increases in old age pensions, together wi-th elimination of the means test and a reduction in the pensionable age.
(d)	Adequate provision for -all disabled adults.
(e)	Selective subsidies, especially on food products and necessities of living.
Before sitting down, I should like to emphasize to hon. members opposite that they are fully conscious of the fact that this amendment embodies the demands which are now being made by the people back home. They know it. This is their opportunity to prove 
that they are conscious of their demands and that they are prepared to support them. I am much afraid that those who oppose the amendment can be charged by the people back home with closing their eyes to their demands and supporting the party.

I first want to make a brief comment, Mr. Speaker, on the amendment which has been moved. Yesterday afternoon the house voted on an amendment I moved sometime ago in effect asking for the reimposition of price controls and subsidies. The government and the house have not approved that proposal. Consequently, under the circumstances under which most of the Canadian people now live, with the climbing costs of living and the insufficiency of wages, salaries, pensions and so on. to meet the increased cost of living, it seems to me that my hon. friends of the Social Credit party have moved an alternative which must be considered by both the government and the house. If you are not going to prevent the costs of living from rising, of necessity you must give these groups to whom I have referred more in the way of purchasing power in order to buy the necessities of life. Consequently, as an alternative to the suggestion that we made to the house, we shall support that amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I was not able to be present last Friday night when some reference was made to this bill. I do not wish to go over the ground covered by the sponsor of the bill, who quoted from the Canada Year Book and gave some of the history of the venture. He did not tell
Bell Telephone Company

the house that this matter had been before parliament in 1928. The company has not expended all the money which it now has. It is proposed to increase the capital by $350,000,000, which will give it a total capitalization of half a billion dollars.
This company operates a monopoly which concerns every telephone user in Ontario and Quebec. Some of the other provinces have telephone systems of their own. When the hydro electric movement was under way back in 1907 and 1908 it was proposed by Sir Adam Beck to have public ownership, not only of light and power, transportation and radials, but of telephones. It was proposed that the same poles would carry the wires for the radial railways, the telephones, the electric light and all that kind of thing. A good job was accomplished in the province in the way of providing cheap power and light, but unfortunately the rest did not go through.
The subject matter of Bill No. 8 was before the House of Commons in 1928. At that time the bill was opposed by some of the newspapers in the Toronto district, because permission was being asked to increase the capital from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000. In 1928 an elaborate discussion of this matter took place in this house lasting for many weeks and months. In considering the principle of this bill you will have to look into the history of the company from the time of its inception. This company has a subsidiary known as Northern Electric, which at that time was a United States trust.
When I first entered parliament in 1921 this proposal was before the house. The first application to amend the Railway Act was made in 1907, 1908, 1909 and 1910. At that time the board of railway commissioners had no jurisdiction over express and telephone companies. After a long fight led by some of the Toronto papers, by the late W. F. Maclean, M.P., and by myself as an alderman, the Railway Act was amended to give the board of railway commissioners jurisdiction over express and telephone companies.
An application was made under that particular act by the city of Toronto to the board of railway commissioners. An elaborate investigation was carried out by Clarkson, Dilworth and Company, chartered accountants. I would refer the house to Hansard of April 10, 1928. The discussion on the bill to increase the capital to $150 million went on for several months and finally it was put over by this house until the 1929 session.
I should like to look at this bill for a few moments to see what it proposes to do. This bill was introduced last December in another place but no section of it received any detailed

examination or consideration there. It was read a second time, without any practical discussion, and referred to a committee. There was no discussion and then it came back on January 29 and was. read the third time without a word of explanation. That type of proceeding is not in the interests of the high court of parliament, especially when it concerns giving this monopoly company power to increase its capitalization to half a billion dollars at a time when it does not need all that money and cannot get parts or equipment for a long time under the export and import dollar plan.
The company has enough money left to carry on all the work it can do for a year yet, and under Bill No. 3, which deals with exports and imports and other regulations, it cannot get parts. It cannot get material and many people cannot get telephones. The discussion the other evening dealt largely with quotations from the annual speech and report of the president and others of the Bell Telephone Company delivered at the annual meeting held recently. The estimate of expenditures for the next five years is as follows:
Right of way	 $	1,233,000
Land and buildings	 42,200,000
Central office equipment ....	96,855,000
Station equipment	 94,607,000
Exchange lines	 86,518,000
Toll lines	 25,605,000
General equipment	 14,630,000
Total	 $361,738,000
Dear knows where we shall be at the end of that time. As I said, away back in 1908 and 1909 it was proposed by Sir Adam Beck (hat telephones should be brought under the cheap light and power movement in Ontario. In 1928 I had the support of an old Liberal paper, the Toronto Globe. At that time the Toronto Globe was a good Liberal paper. At that time the question of the Northern Electric Company, which was a subsidiary of a United States company, was brought up. At that time the board of railway commissioners had no jurisdiction over the Northern Electric Company. A bill was brought before parliament to give the board jurisdiction, not only over the telephone company but over its subsidiary, the Northern Electric Company. I would refer hon. members to Hansard of May 18, 1928, page 3136, where there appear extracts on the Bell company application from the proceedings before the board of railway commissioners.
It was shown then that the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, through the control of Western Electric, held 43 per cent of the stock of Northern Electric. All patents involved belong to the American Telephone

Bell Tele-phone Company
and Telegraph Company. Under a contract made in 1923 the American Telephone and Telegraph Company get one and a half per cent of the gross revenue of the Bell Telephone Company. That amount was then being paid into the United States company which supplies the equipment needed by this company.
In 1909 the Toronto application came on for hearing before that great chairman of the railway board, the late Mr. Justice Mabee. Let me say that I am not opposed to private enterprise but I am opposed to over-capitalization and public utilities, melons and monopolies, and the more this is looked into the more you will find that what I say is correct. I remember when the Toronto Railway Company, with a light plant, the Toronto Electric Light, was trying to sell these two junk plants to our city for 832,000,000, although not worth a third of it. If that had gone through we would have had to pay twenty-five cents for two tickets on the street railway in Toronto, forever. But a great newspaper in the city of Toronto, the Evening Telegram, defeated it, and in opposing the over-capitalization of this railway, referred to my opposing that proposed purchase deal on the eve of an election in the city, on December 31, 1918, in these terms:
. . . the support which J. Ross Robertson gave to the man who fought the battles of Adam Beck for the cause of hydro progress, and who almost single-handed and alone saved this city from bankruptcy, when T. L. Church beat back the purchase raiders in 1913-14.
If that sale of these two companies to our city had gone through we would have had two tickets for a quarter in the city of Toronto and we would not have owned the T.T.C. railway as we do today under the management of the newly formed Toronto transportation commission.
I would not oppose a reasonable application for increased capital by the Bell Telephone Company. It is a well-managed concern. It has some of the finest officers I know in the Toronto district. I would not complain about granting a reasonable increase of, say $100,000,000 for the next three years. That is all it needs, and it does not need even that much. It has enough capital to do it until the next session of parliament.
As I said, the Bell Telephone Company made application to increase its capital stock from 875,000,000 to $150,000,000 in 1928. An amendment was moved to limit the increased capitalization. The intention of the company was to split a melon of $75,000,000 on a five-to-one basis, and Ontario was to be made the goat of a melon split and to pay eight per cent a year, whereas the company's bonds got only 2J per cent.
The Drayton-Acworth royal commission in 1917-18 inquired into the question of overcapitalization of railway companies, express companies and telephone companies, and they recommended that before any applications for increased rates or capitalization were granted by parliament they should be reported on by the board of railway commissioners for Canada. That recommendation has been violated in the present application. In the company's application in 1928 for increased capital the board of railway commissioners found that the Northern Electric Company, a subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company, was outside its jurisdiction and could not be required to submit its records for inspection. The then member for South Toronto, Mr. vjeary, luuuuii^cu a um in the 1028 session to amend the Railway Act to grant the railway commission power in relation to the investigation of subsidiaries of telephone or telegraph companies, like the Northern Electric. The bill proposed that section 375 of the Railway Act, chapter 170 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, be amended accordingly. The government of Ontario, with the city of Toronto, strongly opposed the application of the Bell Telephone Company to increase its capitalization to $150,000,000, and split a melon in Ontario. Their position is set out on page 1896 of Hansard of April 10, 1928. The discussion went on for days and months in the house, with the Ontario government opposing the application for more capital stock and for increased rates. The Ontario government was represented before the railway commission by Mr. Reid, who did well there. He saw fit to write a letter to the Toronto Globe, which was considered then to be the mouthpiece of the Liberal party, although, as I said in 1928, it had latterly been somewhat critical in its attitude toward its old-time friends. The Liberal party deserted Liberal principles. The Globe then was a supporter of public ownership of public utilities in Ontario, such as light, power and transportation, and telephones. Did the government lay down any policy in 1928 with respect to this handout, increasing the capital stock from $75,000,000 to $150,000,000? It was just a huge melon of $75,000,000 to be cut at the expense of telephone users in the city of Toronto and of all Ontario.
Of course the Bell Telephone Company has the right to operate under fair and proper conditions. When the application in 1909, during my term as alderman, came before the late Mr. Justice Mabee, I pointed out that it does not cost any more for your electric light because you are farther away from the power house; that it does not cost you any more
Bell Telephone Company

for your water because you are farther away from the pumping station; that it does not cost you any more for your gas because you are farther away from the gas house; and the chairman of the commission saw the point immediately. On the other hand, why should it cost you more for your telephone if you live farther away? It is just a system of poles, wires and electric instruments, and the free use of highways. There was a difference in the rates paid in many parts of Toronto in those days, north of Bloor, in Deer Park, North Toronto and many other parts now incorporated in the city.
I am speaking without preparation, but I remember in 1928 that Mr. Commissioner Lawrence of the railway commission asked some questions of the representatives who were opposing the application. The railway commission, under Mr. Justice Mabee, ordered a flat rate for telephone service for the whole of greater Toronto, reducing the rate from $75 in some parts of the city-I am speaking from memory-to $30, and I think $40 to $50 for business telephones. Deer Park and on up to Mount Pleasant cemetery on Yonge street were paying that higher figure, but a flat rate was ordered for the whole city. The telephone users in the riding of Davenport, which I used to represent in this bouse, were paying a very large sum for residential and business telephone service. If we had men like Mr. Justice Mabee, who was a strong chairman of the railway commission, there would be no objection to a reasonable increase in the capital stock of the Bell Telephone Company. I am not objecting to a reasonable increase, but I am objecting to over-capitalization and melon splitting.
In this country great corporations have acquired franchises with their heavy rates in light, power and transportation. We found that out in Ontario and in Toronto. We had to pay $32,000,000 for the power companies in the Niagara district. We took them over a few years ago, in 1921, and today, compared with rates under private ownership, rates for commercial and domestic lighting are about one-third of what they used tp be. The money is put back into the pockets of the consumers, and power at cost established for the people.
Under our system of parliamentary government the consumer seems to be the forgotten agency. In recent years he has become the forgotten man. You do not consider him at all, but he is paying the taxes. I have been a supporter of reasonable private enterprise, but want it humanized, and with cheaper rates. I am not going to speak any further tonight. The bill is going to a committee. I would

ask the house not to pay too much attention sometimes on bills like this to what they see in the newspapers. I had five of the six papers opposed to me when I opposed the purchase follies and when we were trying to take over the street railway. An effort was being made to sell a railway and electric light plant for $32,000,000, although they were not worth a third of it. They nearly got it through. The late Sir William Mackenzie was getting franchises all over this country. He was overcapitalizing and putting duplicate lines across the country. He was a skilled parliamentary diplomat and artist, but he found one city where he could not get past the ratepayers on his purchase deals.
I warn this house that if it authorizes this company to increase its capitalization to half a billion dollars it will mean an increase in tolls, and it is good-bye and good night to any chance of having any control or regulation for ever over this utility. Mind you, this is a very fine public utility. I have already said that. I know some of the officers and directors. It is well officered and well handled. During the discussion on Bill No. 3 the other day I congratulated them on one thing, namely, on their permitting their employees to get some of the capital stock and have better labour conditions. It is no wonder they can hand out some of their stock. The stock is to be split up and all that kind of thing.
I have given my reasons why I oppose this bill. We are on very dangerous ground to propose any such thing as capitalizing this company to the extent of half a billion dollars. They do not need it now. It is for five years, they say, to construct. We do not know who will own the country in five years the way things are going. We do not know whether we shall be here or not if we believe everything of the grave danger that the country is in today in foreign affairs. The leaders of the British parliament have already warned us of this gravity. This bill should go to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I do hope that that committee will give the bill better consideration than rvas given it in the other place the other day where they passed it in a very few minutes with no discussion on second reading, no discussion on third reading and all that kind of thing.
I ask for fair treatment for those who are opposing the bill. We do not expect to secure any advantage out of opposing the bill. It would be far better if I did not oppose the bill; it would be far better to leave it to some of the young members in the house who are

Bell Telephone Company
on so many committees, and in whom I have every confidence to protect the consumer.
As a supporter of the principle of public ownership of certain utilities, may I say that Ontario has been made the goat by this overcapitalization. We saw what happened in cheap light and power development and how it worked to the advantage of the consumers in Ontario. What was done there is just an example to the people of this country. Under over-capitalization the people do not own anything. The people should recover their heritage. After all is said and done, these magnificent natural resources of this country do not belong to United States capitalists; they belong to the people of this country and to all the people of the country. Political parties sometimes forget that this magnificent heritage is the property of all the people of Canada. That is what is causing so much communism in the country. There is a lot of talk about communism. While we here have not been friends of the communists, over-capitalization, high rates, putting large profits into the pockets of some of those who are making splits, the high cost of living and all that kind of thing, are factors in causing communism. That is one of the reasons for it. That doctrine has been preached in some of the pulpits of the country. You cannot blame them for getting down to brass tacks today when we see the things happening which I have mentioned.
From the Ottawa river to the Nipigon, the whole of new Ontario, to whom does it belong today, the mines, the waterpowers, the great natural resources, gold, copper, silver, platinum, lead, zinc, everything? Just get some of the financial books and see who owns it and where it is underwritten, not in Canada but in New York. While I welcome capital from everywhere to develop Canada, I believe in the policy of Canada for Canadians, for our own workmen, our own profits for our own people.
I do not object to newspaper criticism; far from it. I got nothing ibut criticism in the fight we had in Ontario and in our city. I am not asking for any favours. I strongly object to this parliament in the dying hours of parliament, because we shall not be here very much longer, giving this company half a billion dollars. The present parliament will cease to be a parliament before long. There will be an election, no doubt, at the proper time. I do object to giving this company $100 million increase. For what? They do not need it this year or for five years. If you gave them about $75,000,000 it would be more than they 5849-123
need for the next three years. The bill which had to do with exports and imports prohibits them from getting any material from the United States, anyway.
I ask for fair, square, honest, honourable consideration of this bill on its merits. Do not forget this: you have to be fair to the people who bore the burden of the day, and also the consumers. The Bell Telephone Company was a splendid organization during the war. It has good officials and directors; they are public-spirited citizens. I have no objection to them at all. This is one of the occasions when we should have a strong board of transport commissioners. If we had they could deal with these problems and would see that justice was given on the merits of the case. For that reason I have made these few remarks. Later I hope to make some further remarks, and I hope that perhaps other hon. members will say something about the matter.

This bill deserves more than a cursory discussion in this house on second reading. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, this is an important bill respecting an increase in the capitalization of a very powerful, and if I may say so, a very efficient company, from $150 million to $500 million. That is an increase of $350 million in one bill. Since I have been in this house I know of no bill that has been passed which, has permitted such an increase in capitalization as the bill now before us.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), who has just taken his seat, on his long service to the country in defending public ownership of important utilities. I do not know of anyone in the country who has more consistently, in this house and outside it, supported the principle for which he has pleaded tonight than the hon. member for Broadview. I sometimes think it is strange that a gentleman who is a member of the Progressive Conservative party should be such a strong proponent of public enterprise. I do remember, of course- and I sometimes refer to it-that the great hydro-electric system in Ontario was largely established by gentlemen who shared the views of the hon. member for Broadview, and I only wish that that had been the trend of that party throughout the years.
Had it been, that party would have been in perhaps a very much different position from that in which it finds itself today. This bill will, of course, be carefully considered by a committee of this house, and I think all
Bell Telephone Company

the details of this proposal should be inquired into with extreme care by the members of that committee.
There is, however, one new clause in this bill to which I wish to refer particularly, and that is paragraph 5 on page 3 of the bill. It reads thus:
It is hereby declared that subject to the provisions of the Radio Act, 1938, chapter fifty of the statutes of 193-8 . . .
And so on, the company has had and always will have the power to- operate and furnish wireless telephone and radio-tele'phone systems and to provide services and facilities for the transmission of messages of various sorts which are enumerated in the bill, over wireless and radio. The explanation given reads:
This section is new. The purpose of this provision is to clarify the company's p-mvers under its original act of incorporation with regard to the use of the latest and most improved means and inventions, including radio and wireless telephone and television in furnishing communication service and will make clear the company's position with regard to the use and operation of radio and wireless telephone in furnishing service to mobile stations and. to remote communities where the construction of wire facilities may be 'impracticable and in interconnecting its wire facilities with radio links.
This is an important new section in this bill that should not be passed over lightly. In the radio committee, from time to time, I have quoted a great deal from speeches of various hon. members who were here when the Radio Act was passed and particularly perhaps from the speeches of the then leader of the opposition, the late Viscount Bennett, then the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. Hon. gentlemen who were here at the time that Mr. Bennett dealt with radio will remember how he used to make this chamber ring with challenges to members of the house to deny that if we had to do over again many of the things we had already done in relation to the great resources to which the hon. member for Broadview referred a few moments ago we would not do what our predecessors did, that is to say, alienate out of the public domain control over great public properties in this country.
Here we have tried throughout the years to see to it that the control of the air waves, as far as this house would agree, and it agreed fairly well, would be such that we would not give away any further this great public facility or allow it to pass into private hands. To my mind this is an important section, and, if this bill is referred to the appropriate committee of the house, then I suggest that this particular provision, section 5, should be referred to the

special committee which I presume will be set up to deal with radio matters, so that the Department of Transport, appearing there as trustee of the air waves in the licensing of stations and so on, shall have an opportunity of discussing this with the committee; that the parliamentary committee be made thoroughly aware of what this clause actually means, and that the representatives of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be properly heard.
After all, mentioned in this explanation of clause 5 are facilities that we have not yet put into use in our country. We have mention of television. Television in the course of the next few years may be a much more important facility that it is at the present time. I believe that, as experimentation goes on, many of the difficulties which now confront television will be met, and television may become universal, even as the standard band of the radio is at the present time.
With the tremendous development in radio and telephonic and telegraphic communication, this bill deserves much more consideration than it has had tonight. A feature of it that has been emphasized is the financial aspect of the matter, the fact that we shall permit, if we pass this bill, a very powerful company to increase its capital from $150 million to $500 million.
As the hon. member for Broadview said a few minutes ago in the course of his speech, in 1928 the extent of the increase was from $75,000,000 to $150 million. That in itself was a substantial increase, but now from $150 million this bill would give the company the power to increase its capitalization to $500 million.
I believe that when a corporation- gets to the point of being a half-billion dollar concern, owning what must be by its very nature a monopoly, it should be a public enterprise and not a private monoply. Some in this house may disagree with my colleagues and myself regarding our ideas on socialization o-r public ownership, but I do not believe that, sitting anywhere in this house, there is an hon. gentleman who really believes in monopoly control. Sometimes the actions of parliament encourage the setting up of monopoly or even the extension, of monopoly, but I do not believe there is anyone in this house who really believes that private monopoly is a good thing.
If we must have monopoly under our economy, the way in which it has developed over the last century or so, with the uniting of small businesses into big businesses, with the growth of public utilities such as we have

Bell Telephone Company
in the company now asking these rights or privileges-that is the better word-from us, I say that, since that development has occurred, we must safeguard the Canadian people against monopoly, and the only safe way, in my opinion, is this. When a monopoly is in the position that this monopoly is in, of controlling a great public facility, then surely the time comes when it should become a public utility.
That being the case, when we allow the company to increase its capital from $150 million to $500 million, what we actually do is to make it more difficult for the province of Ontario or for our own country, Canada, to take over a huge utility like this, because the larger the capitalization, when the time comes to arrive at an agreement with them for compensation, either through expropriation and the legal procedures, or by mutual arrangement, whichever you will, the very size of the sum involved makes it difficult for legislatures or parliament to face the situation that has been created.
When we pass a bill of this description, with $500 million of capitalization, what we are doing is actually placing a barrier against our successors if they desire to take over this facility. We are placing a barrier against their doing so, making it more difficult in the years to come for the nation or the province to take over this great facility.
Those of us who come from provinces in which we own our telephone systems know perfectly well that we enjoy a rate which is better than the one we get in the city of Ottawa. I sometimes compare the rate I have to pay between, we will say, this city and the city of Montreal with the rate I pay between the city of Regina and the city of Saskatoon.
Why not compare the rates and the service in Great Britain?

Just a minute. Saskatoon is nearly twice as far; as a matter of fact. Saskatoon is about 200 miles from Regina and Montreal is about 120 miles from this city. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) says to compare the service.
Certainly.
I would say the service we get from the publicly-owned utility in my province is just as good.
Better.
One of my hon. friends says "better".

He is
prejudiced.

Maybe that is so. But let me point this out to those who are inclined to interrupt. The public ownership of the telephone system in my province and in the neighbouring provinces of Alberta and Manitoba is not the child of any socialistic government. It was set up years ago and it is so good that the Bell Telephone Company would like to buy those facilities. I think I can say without fear of contradiction, and without belittling the services we get from the Bell Telephone Company that the telephone systems in these provinces are as efficient and give as excellent service as anything that will be found anywhere else in Canada.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
Is the hon. member aware of the conditions of the telephone system down in the lower St. Lawrence area and in New Brunswick?
No.
Then it would give the hon. member an argument for the contention he is making, because it is one of the most amazing things in this country.
I like to talk about something about which I know. I greatly regret to say that I do not know as much as I should like t>o know about the lower St. Lawrence.
I will let you know about it later on in this session.

The hon. member who asks me about the lower St. Lawrence perhaps does not know as much as he would like to know about the western provinces in which I have made my home for a good many years. I would suggest to him that, when I resume my seat, he can tell us what kind of service is received along the lower St. Lawrence. If that is accompanied by a description of the beautiful countryside in that area, as an inducement to our going there and examining the telephone system, I am quite sure that hon. members will enjoy the description of that beautiful part of Canada.
But coming back again to my point, let
me say that our telephone systems in our western provinces have not only been of great value to our communities and to our people there, but given good returns to the provinces and assisted us in that way. I sometimes think -and I believe the Minister of Agriculture
Speaker's Ruling

(Mr. Gardiner) whom I see in his seat, and who, incidentally, had a great deal to do with the development of the telephone system will agree-that the conditions under which the people are working within the Saskatchewan telephone system are equal to the best conditions that can be found in telephone businesses anywhere in Canada. As I said a few moments ago, I am drawing these things to the attention of the house-not only the large increase in capitalization but that one important section which hon. gentlemen should examine, namely, section 5, which not only gives to this company a new right but indicates clearly that it is not a new right; they have had it all the time. Since we have had the Radio Act in existence in this country for a long time, and since we have endeavoured at all times to retain control of the air waves, that is a feature of this bill which should not only be considered by the committee to which it is proposed to refer it, but be considered by any committee that is set up to examine radio, television and all these subsidiary matters that concern radio and allied facilities.
The hour reserved for private bills having expired, the house will revert to the business under discussion at six o'clock.

And in 1945 may I remind hon. members that Mr. Tim Buck published large advertisements in the newspapers across Canada urging support for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Liberal party, and so far as I know that was never repudiated'.
On this recent occasion fortunately I am on the record. Mr. Tim Buck spoke in Toronto on the night of January 22-
