Yes, and on that very night I gave to the press this statement which I am going to put on the record :
In the 19451 elections, Canada's communist party'-the L.P.P.-called on the Canadian people to support Mr. Mackenzie King and the Liberals. Today the party has switched its line agiain, and is now declaring its support for the C.C.F.
It is clear to me that the new switch in the communist line is an admission of the utter failure of the Labour Progressive party to make any progress in Canada and of its loss of support even in those trade unions in which the communists have had dominant control hitherto. They are apparently trying ito halt their party's decline by seeking to identify themselves with the C.C.F.
Naturally, what Canadian communists decide to do is entirely up to them. But I want to make the position of the C.C.F. crystal clear. That position has been stated, and re-stated by national and provincial conventions throughout the years.
The C.C.F. will not collaborate with the Labour-Progressive party in any way, direct or indirect. It will not enter into any electoral arrangements with it or with any other party, whether on a national, provincial, or constituency basis.
There is a fundamental difference between, the C.C.F. methods and1 philosophy and those of the communists. We have always opposed', and oppose today, every form of dictatorship, including communist dictatorship. We abhor communist methods in crushing political opposition whenever and whereveT communists become the dominant force in a country.
We know that at bottom the communists have not changed their views about the C.C.F. and democratic socialism. They have always declared democratic socialist movements to be their principal enemy and their ultimate objective is to "liquidate" such movements as the C.C.F.
The present communist policy is therefore just a manoeuvre. The C.C.F. will have nothing to do with it.
That was my statement on the night of January 22. Since then there has been a meeting of the national executive of the C.C.F., and I am quoting from the minutes which I have in my hand.
The executive unanimously endorsed the recent public statement by M. J. Coldwell with respect to the new Labour-Progressive party line.
If that is not about as clear a repudiation as can be made I do not know how it could be made clearer. I wanted to place that on the record of this house in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to where we stand on this particular issue.
Ever since this movement was formed I have been connected with it. At various times we have been the target of abuse and attack by the communist party. At various times

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
they have tried to enter into some collaboration with us. But I want to say this very clearly, in all these years never at any time have we compromised our position; and I am quite certain of this, as long ?s those of us who today have anything to do with the C.C.F. are associated with that party, there will be no association or compromise with the Labour Progressive or communist party, certainly not to the extent that the Liberal party was compromised by the communist party in 1945.
As far as my hon. friends to the right were concerned at that time, I remember the secretary of their party gloating over the situation and saying, "Well, this splits the C.C.F. in many of the industrial districts of Canada and we shall benefit by that split." However, be that as it may; whatever the future fortunes of the Canadian people and of this particular party may be, it is certain that we shall keep our hands clean and our skirts clear of any association with any totalitarian group, whether they are fascistly or communistically inclined.
I want to say a word, Mr. Speaker, about the matter of commercial rents. This afternoon I attempted to raise the question and I accepted the ruling of Your Honour, although, had this debate taken another course, I might have been prevented from raising the issue in time. Perhaps I did not make it quite clear this afternoon, but today is March 5 and the controls come off on Monday, March 8. The intervening period of time between now and Monday is the week end, and during the week end there will certainly be no opportunity for discussion by representatives of the people in this house, and I doubt very much whether there will be much time for the government to consider the situation.
I was disappointed in the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) this afternoon. Under the conditions that exist in regard to commercial rents I do not think we can trust to the individual to take the initiative with the wartime prices and trade board. If he does so, even in the large number of instances of which I have some knowledge at the moment, the wartime prices and trade board will be so busy reviewing complaints made to it that there will be no opportunity for the board to do many of the other things that are vitally necessary at this time.
As I said, I am not going to make a long speech tonight. I stand by the statement I made at the opening of my remarks. I suggest to hon. gentlemen that they will find a great deal of material placed on the record by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) on December 12 last, to be found at pages 264 and 265 of Hansard. What the hon. member did on that occasion was to place before the house a number of complaints that he had received mainly from one city, Winnipeg, showing that the small business people who had occupied premises, in some instances for a good many years, were finding increases in rental of 200 per cent, 300 per cent and 400 per cent, even in some instances after adjustments had been made a year or two ago by the rentals control board in the city of Winnipeg. I have before me a sheaf of letters and telegrams, that I picked at random in my office, and that I have received among many within the past few days. Let me give a sample from Montreal:
Due to the relaxation of Tent control I am now being forced out of business. My landlord is demanding 450 per cent increase in rent.

Here is another small businessman whose landlord is demanding $300 a month increase in the individual's rent. Here is another telegram. These have been received during the last two diays. This man is to have his rent increased by 375 per cent, an increase that the small businessman cannot possibly meet. If this is universal-and I believe it is-then the small businessman will have to charge to the consumer of the goods that are sold in his store an amount equivalent to the increase in rent, and what we actually shall have as a result is a substantial increase in the cost of living.
I have another letter from a man in Toronto whose present rent is $75 a month. He is being asked $250 a month. I have one from the Retail Merchants' Association in my own province of Saskatchewan, from the city of Saskatoon. The letter says:
We are receiving many complaints in this province from merchants who have been asked to increase their payment on rent and in many cases to viaoate.
In the case of vacating and moving to a new location, businessmen find that not any space is available and they are therefore forced to accept the proposal of increased rent.
Would you therefore use your influence and vote endeavouring to have commercial rent control extended for a further period?

Surely those legislatures will do whatever is necessary to protect the population of their provinces against the rapacity- I think that is an exaggeration-of landlords. I admit that there may be hard cases, that there will always be people who will attempt to be unfair, but the great majority of landlords are businessmen. They want good tenants, and they know that the amount that they can derive as rental from their premises is limited to what is fair and just. A few people may attempt to exceed those limits, but we have in all jurisdictions legislation which controls the rapacity of the individual.
For instance, we have a law against usury. It so happens that interest falls within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. No person may collect more than a stated amount of interest. I am confident that if parliament abandons this inter-meddling in affairs which are beyond its jurisdiction, other legislative bodies quite as patriotic, quite as well endowed and quite as capable as that which is within the hearing of my voice, will deal with the question and deal with it promptly and properly. We will put an end to this fictitious system that is bedevilling this house and this parliament. If we have witnessed in the last few weeks episodes within this house which anj-one who cherishes its tradition cannot but regret, it is largely because we have attempted to deal with matters beyond our jurisdiction and have attempted to exercise powers that are not properly within the scope of the powers of this body.
Just so long as there is this interference with normal and free transactions, there is bound to be a shortage of all kinds of buildings which require the investment of money. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has stated that many of the commercial buildings in the city which he represents so well in this house are in the use of the government. I am not going to labour that question, but I will tell the hon. gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches-I see opposite gentlemen from my own city who know the facts as well as I do-that commercial buildings where finance, where commerce and where industry were formerly housed are now filled with government employees, with people who should not be in the service' of the government, people who are attempting under the guise of an emergency to do for the citizenry what the citizenry is well capable of doing for itself. We shall not have new commercial buildings. The capital necessary to put up new commercial buildings required for the normal tenancy of those who are engaged in the growing business of the country will not come forth for investment so long as there is such uncertainty concerning the return which will come from such buildings.
We have heard a good deal about the hardship on the tenant. There may be hard cases for tenants; there inevitably will be. But nobody seems to have said very much about the hardship on the landlord, I think every man of business experience knows there are scores of landlords who attempted to assist weak businesses which were trying to regain their balance after the trying days of the 1930's, who find themselves with rentals frozen at a rate which was entirely unfair to the investor.

Unfortunately at the present time the best of feeling does not exist between the federal government and all the provinces. But the point I make is that this still does not as a general thing in this Dominion of Canada solve the needs of either tenant or landlord until the government does something. This is not now a matter of the British North America Act. We are still in a building materials emergency. Obviously we have not given concern to the adequate supply of building materials so that the small merchant or professional or businessman can construct such premises as he would put up if the supplies were adequate. However, the government must take the whole blame because of its decontrol policy on all these matters.	,
I intend to leave this suggestion with the government. Instead of putting the onus on the tenant, who, generally speaking, has less adequate means whereby to present a proper case before the authorities, who may or may not act in the matter, I suggest that the Minister of Finance send out telegrams to his local offices of the wartime prices and trade board or get on the radio, as he did on November 17, and make an announcement to the effect that commercial rentals-, mind you, the same thing could be said in the case of domestic rentals, because many injustices are being suffered by the small landlord in the case of domestic rentals-shall remain as they were, and that where the landlord considers that his situation is untenable, the onus be put on him, for a change, to take his case to the proper judicial authorities whom the Minister of Finance will designate, and that the landlord, for a change-

The leader of this group tried at three o'clock this afternoon to raise this question, because our members are all convinced that this is a matter of urgent public importance; and in view of the fact that we could not discuss it at that stage, members on all sides are anxious that those who feel strongly should have full opportunity to express their opinions.
We have all had telegrams from people back home who realize that on Monday of next week there will be another factor boosting the cost of living; and in view of the fact that a committee of this house has been appointed to examine and report from time to time as to the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living, I think it is unfortunate that the cabinet should have resisted so stubbornly the representations made to have the whole question referred to the committee.
Technically, this factor has not yet caused any rise in the cost of living, but by Tuesday of next week I think this will be a question which might quite legitimately be referred to the committee. It will cause a great deal of confusion in Canada to have the government's action taken on March 8 brought to the attention of the people, when all across Canada we shall have the tenant exposed to drastic rental increases which will be legal.
I might say to the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) that when I interrupted him a few minutes ago I had no desire to be facetious. I have the greatest respect for his views, and I merely thought he would give some information to support his claim that many landlords in Canada are experiencing real hardships. I know there are cases where landlords have a real grievance, but in view of the fact that many other members this evening went out of their way to show what will happen to the tenants, I thought someone in the house might present the landlord's case.
There are Very few in this house who seriously argue that it was not in the public interest in Canada to have rent controls during the war. I would say to the hon. member for Stanstead that, had he been in

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I had understood that there was a general desire in the
house to have the committee on veterans affairs established as soon as possible. As I said last night, if we had concluded this debate today at an earlier hour, the government had intended to have the house go on to the consideration of setting up that committee. I am entirely in the hands of the house. If hon. members would like to have that committee set up soon, the government is quite prepared to set apart Monday for debate on that question. But if the debate ran beyond Monday we would wish to resume with other government business on Tuesday. On the other hand, if there is exception to having the veterans affairs committee set up on Monday, we shall continue with this debate until it is concluded and then take up the setting up of the committee afterwards.
If the government wishes to proceed with the veterans affairs resolution on Monday, it will be acceptable to us on this side.
As far as our group are concerned, we would be prepared to have the veterans affairs committee set up on Monday.
That is quite acceptable to us.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am pleased to hear that. Then it is understood that we proceed with the veterans affairs resolution. But if that debate runs past Monday, we shall on Tuesday resume other business. If it is concluded during the day, we shall then resume the debate we have been having this evening.
